statement: Among people who use ecstasy, those who have used more of it have lower serotonin transporter binding, in most but not all of the studies that looked. In 24 people scanned with [11C]DASB, binding fell with the logarithm of lifetime tablets in every region but the midbrain: a doubling of lifetime tablets went with a fall of 0.021 binding-potential units in neocortex (95% CI -0.029 to -0.014, p<0.001), 0.062 in pallidostriatum (-0.103 to -0.021, p=0.005), and about 0.07 in thalamus and amygdala (Erritzoe et al., 2011). In 49 people with ecstasy confirmed in hair, the only variables that predicted lower cortical binding were years of use and the largest dose taken in one session (F(2,44)=9.57, p<0.0001), and years of use also predicted lower caudate binding (Kish et al., 2010). In 23 people, global binding was related to the typical monthly dose (r about 0.38, reported as inverse, p=0.04, one-tailed) (McCann et al., 2005), and in a SPECT study the relation with lifetime tablets held in women (r=-0.33, p=0.048) but not men (Reneman et al., 2001). Two studies found no relation: 13 people, where the correlations ran in the same direction but did not reach significance (r about -0.46, p=0.11 to 0.12) (Urban et al., 2012), and the prospective cohort, in which nobody had taken more than 80 tablets and most had taken one or two (de Win et al., 2008). All of these are relations within self-selected groups, measured against lifetime use recalled by the person, which in these samples ranges over two orders of magnitude; none is adjusted for other drug use, and heavier ecstasy use goes with heavier use of everything else. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: People who have taken ecstasy more often tend to show less of the serotonin marker on scans. Four studies found this link, and two smaller ones did not. The amounts come from what people remembered taking, sometimes hundreds of pills over years. People who take more ecstasy also tend to take more of other drugs, and none of these studies could separate the two.
population: Adults who use ecstasy recreationally, abstinent when scanned
exposure: More cumulative ecstasy use (lifetime tablets, years of use, typical monthly dose or largest dose in one session)
comparator: Lighter use within the same group
outcome: Serotonin transporter binding measured with PET or SPECT
magnitude: Per doubling of lifetime tablets: -0.021 binding-potential units in neocortex (95% CI -0.029 to -0.014), -0.062 in pallidostriatum (-0.103 to -0.021), about -0.07 in thalamus and amygdala (Erritzoe et al., 2011; on a neocortical control mean of about 0.33 units, a doubling is roughly a 6% fall). Regression of cortical binding on years of use and maximum dose F(2,44)=9.57, p<0.0001 (Kish et al., 2010). Correlations: about 0.38 with typical monthly dose, one-tailed p=0.04 (McCann et al., 2005); -0.33 with log lifetime tablets in women, p=0.048 (Reneman et al., 2001); -0.44 to -0.47, p=0.11 to 0.14, not significant, in 13 people (Urban et al., 2012). No relation in the prospective cohort, where the median was 2 tablets (de Win et al., 2008).

evidence.locator: Methods, 'Participants and drug use' (p. 563, the conversion of powder to tablets); Table 1 (p. 564, lifetime tablets); Results, 'SERT binding', 2nd paragraph and Figure 3 (p. 568)
evidence.extracted: In 24 people who used MDMA and/or hallucinogens, binding fell with the logarithm of lifetime MDMA tablets in every region except the midbrain: per doubling of tablets, -0.021 binding-potential units in neocortex (95% CI -0.029 to -0.014, p<0.001), -0.062 in pallidostriatum (-0.103 to -0.021, p=0.005), -0.067 in thalamus (p=0.006) and -0.075 in amygdala (p<0.001). The printed upper limits for thalamus (0.022) and amygdala (0.045) contradict their p-values and appear to be missing a minus sign. Lifetime tablets were self-reported and ranged from 6 to 6590, with powder converted to tablets at 60 mg each.

evidence.locator: Table 2 (p. 1785, lifetime tablets and maximum dose); Results, 'PET [11C]DASB non-displaceable binding potential', 5th paragraph (p. 1787)
evidence.extracted: In a stepwise regression within 49 people with ecstasy confirmed in hair, entering demographic, drug-history, mood, subjective-effect and cognitive variables, the only predictors of lower binding across all cortical regions were years of use and maximum dose per session (F(2,44)=9.57, p<0.0001); years of use also predicted lower caudate binding (F(1,41)=4.91, p=0.032). Lifetime tablets ranged from 4 to 922 (median 126) and maximum dose from 1 to 20 tablets (median 3), by self-report.

evidence.locator: Table 1 (p. 1744, sample); Results, last paragraph (p. 1745, correlations); Discussion (p. 1748, the authors’ caution)
evidence.extracted: In 23 people abstinent from MDMA, global binding (distribution volume ratio) was related to the typical monthly dose for both radioligands (r=0.38 and 0.37, described in the text as inverse, p=0.04 for both), on one-tailed tests chosen in advance; the authors state the study was not powered for these correlations and call them preliminary.

With SPECT and [123I]beta-CIT, overall binding ratio correlated with the logarithm of lifetime ecstasy tablets in women (r=-0.33, p=0.048) but not in men (r=0.07, p=0.699). The text extraction renders the coefficient as 'r=20.33'; the rendered page shows -0.33. (the Lancet prints decimal points as middle dots; the text extraction renders the coefficient as 'r=20·33').

In 13 people, no correlation between binding and any use variable reached significance: with lifetime uses, dorsolateral prefrontal r=-0.46 (p=0.12) and parietal r=-0.46 (p=0.11); with duration of use, occipital r=-0.47 (p=0.12) and parietal r=-0.44 (p=0.14). Lifetime sessions ranged from 15 to 1050 (median 50).

evidence.locator: Results, 'Brain imaging', last paragraph (p. 2939); Discussion, limitations paragraph (p. 2943, the distribution of use)
evidence.extracted: In the prospective cohort, no relation was found between the cumulative number of tablets and any follow-up imaging measure; the authors attribute this to the narrow range of use, since 54% had taken one tablet or less and only 17% ten or more.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 'Serotonin transporter', 2nd paragraph; Discussion, 'MDMA and additional drug use'
evidence.extracted: The review notes that human transporter studies have smaller effect sizes than animal studies (-0.05 to -2.17 against -0.38 to -20.03), that human exposure is estimated at 2-4 mg/kg per tablet-and-a-half session against 20-141 mg/kg in the animal experiments, and that two studies suggest cannabis, cocaine and hallucinogen use do not account for the transporter findings. It records no pooled dose-response estimate.

risk_of_bias.note: Cumulative use is recalled by the person, spans two orders of magnitude within each sample and is not verified for amount; the relations are unadjusted for other drug use, which rises with ecstasy use; several are one-tailed or uncorrected, and all are within self-selected groups.

inconsistency.note: Four studies found a relation and two did not; one of the nulls had 13 participants with correlations of the same size as the significant ones elsewhere, and the other had almost no variation in dose, so the inconsistency is partly explained, but it is not resolved.

indirectness.note: Measured exposure and measured binding, as worded.

imprecision.note: Not downgraded twice: the small samples are already counted under risk of bias and inconsistency.

dose_response.note: Not applied: a dose-response gradient cannot upgrade the claim that there is a dose-response gradient.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low and is downgraded for risk of bias (self-reported lifetime use, unadjusted for other drugs, some one-tailed and uncorrected tests) and for inconsistency (two of six studies found no relation). The direction is the same wherever a relation appears, which is why the claim is made at all; its size is not estimable from these data.

verification.flag_note: Anchors are ai-located and need a second reader. The relation rests on within-group correlations and regressions; no study has measured exposure other than by recall, so a quantitative dose-response cannot be given.

changelog.change: Drafted (AI reader 45, MDMA batch 5a) from six primary imaging studies read in full, with the review for context, to answer whether the transporter difference is larger with more use.
